catalog_quote: [Schachter & Reid] Vowel length in non-word-final syllables is phonemic, as the following examples illustrate: aso /?a:so/ 'dog', aso /?aso/ 'smoke' ... In word-final syllables of native words, vowel length is not phonemic: the general rule is that phrase-final syllables are long, non-phrase-final syllables short. ... Stress is closely tied to vowel length, with some analysts considering stress as primary, while others consider vowel length to be primary. Syllables with phonemically long vowels are always stressed. Syllables with vowels that are not phonemically long but are phonetically long as a result of their occurrence in phrase-final position are also stressed if there are no phonemically long vowels in the phrase-final word. Thus the final syllable of magaling /magaliŋ/ [magali:ŋ] 'excellent' is stressed in citation, but in magaling na /magaliŋ na/ [magaliŋ na:] 'it's excellent n…
sweep_summary: Tagalog (taga1270) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Schachter & Reid 2008. Of the 9 works with stress in the title: Hsieh 2016 (AFLA 23, read from the ANU OA volume) and Nagaya & Hwang 2018 (LangSci OA, read) are phrase-level prosody with no word-stress content (silent); Sabbagh 2014 (read in the lingbuzz preprint) states in passing, citing French 1988, that stress is contrastive and falls on the final or penultimate syllable (confirms). Three direct stress sources could not be read: Gonzalez 1981 'Tagalog accent revisited' (print only, LSP Monograph 2; high priority), French 1988 (the standard monograph every read paper cites; Glottolog's SIL URL is dead and SIL archive 22216 now points elsewhere; print only; high priority), French 1991 'Secondary stress in Tagalog' (JSTOR paywalled, doi 10.2307/3623086; medium). Brichoux 1972 is an 87-page MA thesis (California State College, LA), duplicated in Glottolog, not online (medium). Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Books 3) is open on sil.org but the PDF sits behind an automated-access block that automated download, direct download and headless/Xvfb Chrome all fail; its abstract (saved) treats Tagalog as a morphemic/floating-stress language (medium). Beyond the list, two open 2025 papers were read: Zuraw & Roca (Phonology, already held by the project) give corpus evidence that both penult- and ultima-prominent words bear phonological stress — the best first-hand statement found, refining and arguably superseding the hedged Schachter & Reid quote as the deciding source for 'lexical' — and Farinella & Jun (PLSA, downloaded now) restate unpredictable stress within a right-edge two-syllable window while staying agnostic on stress vs length. all lookups went through APIs (Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Glottolog.bib, Open Library, ANU/lingbuzz/Zenodo) and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: Words in Tagalog/Filipino can be either penult-prominent or ultima-prominent. Scholars have been divided on whether the language has stress, or only phonemic vowel length in penults and default phrase-final prominence. Using a corpus of Original Pilipino Music, we find that both prominent penults and prominent ultimas are set to longer notes and stronger beats, even in phrase-medial position. ... We conclude that songwriters' text-setting decisions reflect phonological stress in Filipino, and that both penult-prominent and ultima-prominent words bear stress. [p. 1] All this is evidence in favour of analysing Filipino as having stress [§10, p. 25]
new_statements.citation: Zuraw, Kie & Paolo Roca. 2025. Evidence for stress in Filipino text-setting. Phonology 42: e7, 1-30. doi:10.1017/S0952675725000041
new_statements.reading: Lexically contrastive word stress restricted to the last two syllables (penult or ultima; minimal pairs like ʔábot/ʔabót, búkas/bukás), with no root-anchored default; a first-hand corpus study concluding that the prominence is phonological stress rather than phonemic vowel length plus phrase-final accent. This supports the catalog's 'lexical' coding and is a stronger deciding statement than the hedged Schachter & Reid 2008 passage, whose own wording ('vowel length.. is phonemic', 'some analysts considering stress .') sits in the length camp. Caveat: the length analysis is still held by Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 / Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024, as both Zuraw & Roca and Farinella & Jun 2025 record.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No change to the classification: lexical (prominence lexically contrastive within a right-edge two-syllable window, word-level). Zuraw & Roca 2025 can carry the deciding quotation for "word-level stress, penult or ultima"; keep Schachter & Reid 2008 and Bloomfield 1917 as corroboration for the distributional facts (aso/aso minimal pair, closed-penult ban, phrase-final lengthening, rightward shift before -an/-in), since Z&R's own description of those facts (section 2.2, pp. 3-7) is a synthesis of Gonzalez 1970, Anderson 2006, Klimenko et al. 2010 and Schachter & Otanes 1972, not new fieldwork.…

audit.reasoning: (1) All three deciding/corroborating quotations were found verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators (Schachter/Reid the text layer; Bloomfield secs. 38, 39, 45; H&K ex. 2). (2) The classification rests on a 2008 handbook sketch by the reference-grammar author plus Bloomfield 1917 and the Himmelmann & Kaufman prosody survey; the newly downloaded Zuraw & Roca 2025 (Phonology, open access) restates exactly our classification: two lexical word classes (penult- vs ultima-prominent, minimal pairs ʔábot/ʔabót), penult prominence only on open penults, closed penults repel prominence with loan exceptions, and the only live dispute is stress vs phonemic length as the underlying category -- which our the primary-stress rule already flags. sources.quote: Words in Tagalog/Filipino can be either penult-prominent or ultima-prominent. Scholars have been divided on whether the language has stress, or only phonemic vowel length in penults and default phrase-final prominence. ... We conclude that songwriters' text-setting decisions reflect phonological stress in Filipino, and that both penult-prominent and ultima-prominent words bear stress. (p. 1) — All this is evidence in favour of analysing Filipino as having stress ... We believe that the musical data here provide the first straightforward evidence in favour of one analysis, the stress-driven one. (§10, p. 25)
sources.note: First-hand corpus evidence (1,662-word OPM song corpus): both penult- and ultima-prominent words are set to longer notes and stronger beats even phrase-medially, so word-level prominence is phonological stress, lexically distributed over the last two syllables (minimal pair ʔábot 'power' vs ʔabót 'arrival'; loans with antepenult, e.g. ʔágila). §2.2.2 lays out the two camps: phonemic-length (Constantino 1965; Schachter & Otanes 1972; Soberano 1980; Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020) vs phonemic-stress (Bloomfield 1917; Blake 1925; Ramos 1981; French 1988, 1991; Avery & Lamontagne 1995; Sabbagh 2014; R…

sources.quote: Stress, which is contrastive in Tagalog, generally falls either on the final or the penultimate syllable of a word regardless of the number of syllables (French 1988:63-65). Assuming that stress is associated with the prosodic category Foot, the position of stress in words can be taken to suggest that feet are parsed from right-to-left in Tagalog. Right-to-left parsing of feet will leave any un-footed syllables—e.g., in odd syllable words—to be (stray) adjoined at the prosodic word level. Hence, three syllable words such as siyásat ('investigation') and talagá ('surely') have the schematic prosodic structure shown in (71).
sources.locator: preprint p. 27, §5.4 'Weak Start in Other Domains'
sources.note: Syntax-prosody paper (Weak Start constraint driving verb-initial and Comp-WhP orders). One passing, second-hand statement (citing French 1988) that stress is contrastive and lands on the final or penultimate syllable; treats stress, not vowel length, as the phonological primitive. No new data on stress placement.

sources.quote: Tagalog has a word level relative prominence distinction which has been analyzed as either a vowel length contrast or stress. On the latter analysis, Tagalog roots have unpredictable stress within a two syllable window at the right edge of words (Bloomfield 1917; French 1988). This gives rise to minimal pairs such as /"aso/ (dog) and /as"o/ (smoke). The other approach claims that Tagalog has a vowel length contrast on penultimate syllables in roots (Schachter & Otanes 1972; Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024; Kaufman To appear). ... The purpose of this paper is not to make claims about the word level prosodic system of Tagalog, but about intonation.
sources.note: Intonation study (AP/iP/IP edge tones). Restates the placement fact — unpredictable prominence on penult or ultima, minimal pairs — and the two analyses, stays agnostic on stress vs length; finds AP-initial tones only optionally align to the prominent syllable (Figs 7-8, words with penult and with final 'stress'), i.e. word-level prominence is visible to the intonation system phrase-medially.

sources.quote: Stress is shown to exhibit the following autosegmental properties: stability (Bedouin Hijazi Arabic), morphemic stress (Spanish, Turkish, Tagalog), and the ability to float (Mayo, Tagalog). ... Stressless feet and unfooted stresses are instantiated in Mayo and Tagalog. ... the autosegmental theory of stress facilitates the simple formalization of a number of stress systems with heretofore complex analyses, including Yidiny, Mayo, Cairene Arabic, Turkish, Khalkha Mongolian, Capanahua, and Tagalog.
sources.note: Abstract only: treats Tagalog as a language with lexically specified (morphemic, floating) stress and gives a formal analysis of its stress system; the SIL editor's note calls the work 'outdated in many respects'. The Tagalog chapter itself was not reachable, so the actual placement statement is unverified.
